node.label: Sidney Mintz
node.date_label: Worker in the Cane1960 · Sweetness and Power1985 · Three Ancient Colonies2010
node.description: Sidney Mintz joined Caribbean fieldwork to histories of labour, slavery, markets and consumption. Worker in the Cane presents the narrated life of Eustaquio “Taso” Zayas; Sweetness and Power traces sugar through colonial production and changing diets. With Richard Price he investigated Afro-American cultural formation. Three Ancient Colonies compares Jamaica, Haiti and Puerto Rico. His anthropological training and fieldwork shaped historical inquiries that connect workers’ experiences, Caribbean societies and wider economic change.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Worker in the Cane: A Puerto Rican Life History (1960); Caribbean Transformations (1974); With Richard Price, An Anthropological Approach to the Afro-American Past: A Caribbean Perspective (1976); Sweetness and Power: The Place of Sugar in Modern History (1985); Sweetness and Power — Penguin edition (1986); With Richard Price, The Birth of African-American Culture: An Anthropological Perspective — reissue with new preface (1992); Tasting Food, Tasting Freedom: Excursions into Eating, Culture, and the Past (1996); Three Ancient Colonies: Caribbean Themes and Variations (2010).
node.scope_note: Read Mintz’s three short author essays, selected2013 interview answers published2014, Leslie Rice’s1996 report, and Michiel Baud’s2011 review; complete monographs and the Mintz/Price primary essay and1992 preface remain unread. Baud’s reading of Caribbean Transformations is explicitly mediated, and he cautions that Three Ancient Colonies’s older fieldwork vignettes leave later migration, tourism and other changes insufficiently addressed. Original works, collections and reissues are distinct. Existing IDs, roster prose and source qualifications remain; no complete career interval or universal reception is inferred. incident_edges.relationship: Sugar’s changing uses connect consumption to colonial production and industrial work
incident_edges.evidence_note: Mintz’s “Sugar,” opening paragraphs1–8, explains the historical route from Caribbean fieldwork through a commodity’s global markets and human costs. His primary retrospective supports this scoped contribution; complete Sweetness and Power remains unread.

incident_edges.relationship: A cane worker’s narrated life becomes a perspective on Puerto Rican labour history
incident_edges.evidence_note: In the Thomas interview, sectionIV, Mintz explains returning to work with Taso and constructing a personal account alongside Puerto Rican history. The worker’s interpretation is part of the inquiry. Mintz’s claim to absolute disciplinary priority is not adopted.

incident_edges.relationship: With Richard Price, cultural formation is studied through new circumstances and social institutions
incident_edges.evidence_note: Baud(2011),263, explicitly identifies this joint1976/1992 inquiry. This named reader supports the scoped connection; it does not imply identical Afro-American cultures or prove influence on all Atlantic historians. Joint authorship and distinct editions are retained; primary essay unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Plantation provisioning and peasant activity expose tensions within colonial economic organization
incident_edges.evidence_note: Baud(2011),260, reads Caribbean Transformations as explaining provision grounds and emerging peasant practices within plantation society. This is Baud’s specific account of Mintz’s contribution, not a catalogue-derived argument or a general claim that all customary markets shared one logic.

incident_edges.relationship: Greene credits cooperation with Mintz and Richard Price in sustaining the interdisciplinary Atlantic History and Culture program he helped organize at Johns Hopkins.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own retrospective answer identifies actual Anthropology Department cooperation over several decades and describes the original interdisciplinary program rather than mere shared employment. Richard Price retains joint credit; his endpoint is absent. This is a bounded collaborative intellectual setting, not proof of Mintz’s sole authorship, a specific book debt or personal formation. Precise institutional chronology not independently audited. Philip D.Morgan is a distinct absent-endpoint successor/coeditor, not Edmund S.Morgan.

named_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Publisher description now checked for this specific argument; the full book and reception remain unreviewed.

named_group_routes.relationship: Named ethnographic studies inform Thompson’s questions about time and markets
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Time essay pp. 58–59 uses Evans-Pritchard and Bourdieu; Moral Economy p. 135 invokes Mintz on markets. These are distinct resources, not a uniform anthropological model or proof that his cultural comparisons generalize universally.

named_group_routes.relationship: Van Gennep’s folklore and Douglas on pollution and boundaries, then Evans-Pritchard, Turner, Geertz and Mintz, read for questions tested on sixteenth-century evidence (1969–1980s)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her acknowledgements, in period and in retrospect. 1973 (read): ‘For the theory in this paragraph, I have found helpful Mary Douglas’s remarks on the relation between pollution fears and concern for social boundaries (Purity and Danger … ch. 7)’ (p. 61, n. 25); Van Gennep’s Manuel de folklore français on the dead (p. 57, n. 17). 1997 (read in full): she found Van Gennep’s Manuel, but her essay ‘used only historical evidence’ and, ‘in contrast with the static unchanging portrait of ceremonial and customary life presented in Van Gennep’, ‘pointed to shifts’ (p. 14); ‘I went on to read in anthropology and folklore: E.E. Evans-Pritchard, Victor Turner, Clifford Geertz, Sidney Mintz, and many others … I read eclectically, indifferent to conflicts within anthropology, for I was not looking for solutions, but for questions’ (p. 14); ‘One term I co-taught a course with Clifford Geertz’ (p. 19); the Martin Guerre project ‘grew out of the practice of anthropological history’ (p. 17). Finlay (1988, p. 554, read) attributes the book’s ‘inventive aspects’ to ‘anthropology, ethnography, and literary criticism’. No single anthropologist is credited as the source, and no specifically Geertzian method is established.

sources.citation: Robert Finlay, “The Refashioning of Martin Guerre,” American Historical Review 93, no. 3 (1988): 553–571.

verification.note: Read for revision 1.143 (data/extension-2026/davis-backfill-2026-10-17/evidence-davis.md §5): read in full in a JSTOR scan on a UBC course blog (blogs.ubc.ca/history548/files/2015/09/Finlay-Martin-Guerre.pdf). Quoted: ‘Even within this select company [Le Roy Ladurie, Ginzburg], however, Natalie Zemon Davis’s Return of Martin Guerre is exceptional’ (p. 553); in-period reviews by Moote, Kelley and Le Roy Ladurie (NYRB, 22 December 1983) as Finlay quotes them (p. 554, n. 3; mediated); ‘Davis fails to show that her view of women in peasant society is relevant’ (p. 557); ‘self-fashioning’ ‘merely imposed on the historical record’ (p. 564); ‘it is difficult to see what distinguishes the writing of history from that of fiction’ and the praise of ‘its eloquent portrait of peasant life’ (p. 569); ‘a sort of proto-feminist of peasant culture’ (p. 570); ‘the sovereignty of the sources, the tribunal of the documents … an excess of invention’ (p. 571). Note 71 (p. 569) cites Ginzburg’s postface to the Italian edition (1984), unread.

sources.citation: Natalie Zemon Davis, A Life of Learning: Charles Homer Haskins Lecture for 1997, ACLS Occasional Paper 39 (New York: American Council of Learned Societies, 1997).

verification.note: Read for revision 1.143 (data/extension-2026/davis-backfill-2026-10-17/evidence-davis.md §1): read in full in the ACLS PDF text layer. Printed folios 10–23 appear in the text; folios 1–9 were fixed from the constant PDF offset (PDF page = printed page + 6), checked against 10–23. The unsigned ACLS preface is unpaginated and is a separate reader statement. Passages used: Bloch, Strange Defeat (p. 5) and Feudal Society (p. 7); Marx and Weber tested on Lyon (p. 7); history of the book (p. 10); multiple social axes (p. 11); ‘A Trade Union’ (1966) and Hobsbawm (pp. 12–13); Annales histoire totale ‘could not serve as a model’ (p. 13); Van Gennep, Bakhtin, and reading Evans-Pritchard, Turner, Geertz and Mintz ‘eclectically’ (p. 14); Society and Culture and ‘Rites’ (p. 15); the 1971 course with Jill Conway, ‘the first course in women’s history in Canada’ (p. 16); film and ‘anthropological history’ (pp. 17–18); ‘I came to microhistory (or what I called ethnography) via film’ and co-teaching with Geertz (p. 19); Fiction in the Archives and Stone (p. 21); ‘a decentered comparison of three European lives’ (p. 21); margins and colonial intrusion (p. 22); ‘permanently relocated as an historian of Europe’ (p. 23). Retrospective testimony (1997): evidence of how she later described her work, not of what the earlier works say.

verification.note: Downloaded primary scan: pp. 76–80, 133 and 135 read; text on 134 and 136 was partly clipped and is not treated as completely read. sources.title: E. P. Thompson, “Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism,” Past & Present 38 (1967): 56–97.
sources.citation: E. P. Thompson, “Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism,” Past & Present 38 (1967): 56–97.

verification.note: Downloaded primary scan: opening pp. 56–62 and selected concluding passages pp. 89–97 read; some extracted passages/notes were truncated, so no full-article reading claimed. Explicit resources include Le Goff, Febvre, Evans-Pritchard and Bourdieu. Employment relations complicate task/clock distinctions; education, religion and coercion matter alongside clocks. Concluding criticism of Moore/Kerr/Siegel contests treating workers as inert inputs. Thompson’s own developmental assumptions and cultural comparisons remain situated arguments, not a proven universal sequence.
